**B3 (returns correct shortened string — algorithm):** Judge this item end-to-end: trace the response's code as written, including its loop bounds, its indices, and whatever location it actually finds for the hyphen, and ask whether the method would return the correct shortened string for a typical valid username. Deduct if the end-to-end result would be wrong — for example, a loop bounded by a constant (`i < 10`) or an off index search that makes the final returned string incorrect — even when the substring/concatenation logic is itself textbook; likewise deduct for the listed algorithmic defects: failing to return the string, incorrectly building it (early return, failing to initialize correctly), bounds errors, modifying `username`, or printing the string instead of or in addition to returning it. No_deduct when the string that would actually be returned is correct.

Two kinds of flaws do not count against this item. First, compilation-level slips elsewhere in the method that are unrelated to the algorithm — an undeclared variable, a missing brace, returning a value whose type is slightly off — are excused so long as the intended construction and return of the correct string is unambiguous; deduct only for algorithmic defects in building and returning the shortened string. Second, malformed String method usage — wrong argument order, wrong number of arguments, or a wrong method name, e.g. `username.substring(i, 0)` or `username.subString(0, i)` — falls under the excused "call any String method incorrectly" case rather than being treated as a disqualifying bounds error, and earns no_deduct as long as the intended algorithm (which pieces of the string are combined and returned) is correct.
